utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have the appearances, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, counsel. Appearing for the Prosecution today, Mark Harmon, Salvatore Cannata, and Carmela Javier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. Mr. Perisic is represented today by Mr. Gregor Guy-Smith, Mr. Boris Zorko, and myself, Novak Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Good morning, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just to remind you, once again, that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Understood, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, sir, Mr. Borovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with your leave, I remembered last night the answer to a question that was asked of me both by the Defence and the Prosecution, namely, whether the military office of the president of the republic had a legal officer, and I remembered that in fact the military office of the president had a lawyer on its staff. That's what I wanted to add, if it's of any interest to the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Borovic. Are you able to tell us the name of the lawyer at the time that you were ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that lawyer was Colonel Milivoj Jovic or Jovovic, and we got a young lawyer by the name of Kisic. And I continued to run into that young lawyer later on at the Ministry of Defence. He was promoted and came to the administration. And when I was thinking about various lawyers, I couldn't remember exactly where I knew this Kisic from and where this Milivoj Jovic went on, because he was close to retirement, and I think I remember now he joined the military office of the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Borovic. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, General Borovic.

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, you testified in your earlier evidence about Prosecution Exhibit 2519.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could have 2519 on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document that is dated the 25th of April, 1995, and it is from General Mladic to the General Staff, attention of General Perisic. And I want to examine this request for personnel a little bit. I want to direct your attention to the second item, Lieutenant-Colonel Radoslav Jankovic, and you can see in this request that General Mladic is requesting that Lieutenant-Colonel Jankovic be sent to the VRS Main Staff Intelligence Administration. You can see that in the first part of the letter. And this identifies, does it not, that Lieutenant-Colonel Radoslav Jankovic was currently on duty in the VJ General Staff 2nd Administration?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, according to the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the 2nd Administration was the Intelligence Administration of the VJ; correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, from this letter we can see that Colonel Jankovic, at General Perisic's request, had been temporarily re-assigned to the VRS Main Staff Intelligence Administration, where he had spent two months. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that's written in the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So now if we could turn to Mr. Jankovic's personnel file, which is P269 -- 2696, please. And what I'm interested in is, first of all, looking at the first page to confirm this is Mr. Jankovic's personnel file. We could go to e-court English translation -- there it is in B/C/S. I see it's already on the monitor. And the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And did you say it's P2696?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: P2696, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So we can see from this document this is the personnel file of -- first page of Radoslav Jankovic, colonel; correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we turn to English e-court in the same exhibit 0422-2995 ET, page 2; and in the B/C/S if we could turn to page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, this is part of Colonel Jankovic's personnel file, and we can see his career trajectory. And if we -- if you take a look, General Borovic, you'll see an entry. It is --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can we go -- scroll all the way -- thank you. Could we scroll a little bit over the document so we can see the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, do you see, sir, that the fifth box from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, Mr. Harmon. It doesn't look like we've got the same page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have part of the same page, Your Honour. You'll see there's a reference, Your Honour, at the penultimate entry on the English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- there's a reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Penultimate?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Penultimate entry, there's a reference to the temporary deploy -- temporarily deployed to the 30th Personnel Centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're right, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And then there's some data entered to the right of that. You can find that entry in the B/C/S page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Five entries up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you see this entry, General Borovic, that says temporarily deployed to the 30th Personnel Centre --

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. It says -- let me just read the entry so it's in the record. "Temporarily deployed to the 30th KC," which means personnel centre, "of the General Staff of the VJ garrison Belgrade." It gives a date of 02/06/95. And PSU 200-70 with a date that follows that, that reflects that that was pursuant to an order of the personnel administration of the VJ General Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if we look just above the entries that I referred to, we can see a number of references to -- in the second column, to Colonel Jankovic's career. You'll see that he's in the 2nd Administration, which is the intelligence administration, prior to coming to -- prior to being temporarily deployed to the 30th Personnel Centre; correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the personnel file, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have -- I want to take a look at a film.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We're going to look at a film, General. And this is a film with Colonel Jankovic, General Mladic, and others taken in Srebrenica on the 12th of July. This is Prosecution Exhibit 437.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, for counsel, Colonel Jankovic was identified in P437 as the person seated to the left of General Mladic in this film. That transcript citation reference is 6568, starting at line 15. So if we could then show this film.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would like you to pay attention to this film, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Stop the film, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We now have the same film, the proper segment of the film I wanted to exhibit to this witness. Can you play that, please. This is started at 1:35:40, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: For the record, we've ended the film at 1:41:11.5.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, General Borovic, was the take-over of the Srebrenica enclave by the VRS something that would have had security implications for the FRY, for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe it had, at the international level, adverse consequences for the FRY security because it was our commitment at the time that there should be no further escalation of tensions with the international community as regards the enclaves, but I'm seeing this for the first time. I didn't know these people. The cabinet just sent a letter to the personnel administration to deal with this. I thought it was going to have adverse consequences and it later turned out it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, my question really was answered in part but not fully. The question I asked you was: Would the take-over - not did the take-over but would the take-over - of a UN-protected safe area of Srebrenica by the VRS, would that be something that would have had or would have security implications for the VRS -- for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was not evaluating the situation then. I was only a chef de cabinet. And now I believe that any combat operations close to our border have security implications on our country too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, I know -- I didn't ask you whether you were evaluating the situation then. You're a general in the Yugoslav Army. You were fully aware that the Srebrenica enclave was a protected safe area. You were aware, were you not, that if there was a take-over of the safe area, that that could result in NATO intervention within a kilometre or two of your state border? So did it -- at the time the VRS took over the Srebrenica enclave, did the take-over have, in your opinion, security implications -- at the time it was taken over, did it have security implications for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prosecutor, sir, at that time I was not a general, I was not involved in this, I didn't even know that the enclave of Srebrenica would be attacked. Now in hindsight I believe it was wrong and that NATO bombing did ensue and that it did have negative consequences on the security of our country.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So are you unable to tell us on the 13th of July -- I'm sorry, when the enclave was taken over on the 11th of July, 1995, by the VRS, are you able to give us your opinion, sir, on that date whether that event would have had security implications for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer a question phrased like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's -- let me say -- let me ask you this, sir: You were aware that the Srebrenica enclave was a safe area that was under United Nations protection, you were aware that it was a safe area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And would, in your opinion, sir, on the 12th and 13th of July, would the forcible displacement of 25- to 35.000 inhabitants of the Srebrenica enclave have possible security implications for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I did not know anything about these events. I can say now that it would have security implications and that it was wrong, but at that time we had no information about Srebrenica. None of this information reached the cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, would the murder of thousands of Bosnian Muslim inhabitants from Srebrenica have security implications for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia? You can answer that yes or no. And if you have an explanation you'd like to give after you answer the question, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer yes. It would have negative implications.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, would you expect that a VJ intelligence officer who was assigned to the VRS Intelligence Administration on a temporary assignment to keep the -- his superior unit informed of the operations that were occurring within the Srebrenica theatre of operations?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not expect that, sir, because he was resubordinated to another command to which he was sent, and he had no obligation to keep his original command informed apart from regular reporting along the chain of command at another level and which has no immediate contact with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would you expect a VJ intelligence officer who was assigned to the VRS to inform his superior officers that there were events taking place in Srebrenica that had security implications on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is the same question that was already asked by the witness [as interpreted] rephrased. He said why he didn't expect that officer to do that, because he was resubordinated to another unit; and now Mr. Harmon is trying to get in a different way an answer different to what he originally didn't like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General Borovic, would it, in your opinion, have been responsible of a -- for a VJ officer who was aware of events that could have significant repercussions for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to remain silent about those events?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prosecutor, sir, an officer sent from another administration I think no longer had any connection with the chief of the 2nd Administration. He was connected with the intelligence authorities in the Army of Republika Srpska. It would not have been proper if he had come and been questioned about it. He had no longer any connection with the chief of the 2nd Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me give you a hypothetical situation, General Borovic. Let me put you in the shoes of Colonel Jankovic. Let's assume that you were in Srebrenica on the 12th and the 13th of July, 1995, and you, sir, were aware that the Srebrenica enclave had been taken over; you were aware that 25- to 35.000 Muslim inhabitants from the enclave were forcibly displaced; you were aware that thousands of Muslim inhabitants from that enclave had been murdered. Would you -- and you were aware that those events had security implications for your country. Would you have remained silent?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection to this phrasing. But in order to state my objection, I would not like Mr. Borovic to be present in the courtroom. I don't want to influence him. Could he step out for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, you are -- could you please excuse us for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A question put in this way -- well, first of all, the witness is being asked to speculate about something that is in the intelligence domain. That is why I object to it. We're asking the witness to provide his opinion on exclusively intelligence matters and he has never been an intelligence officer. Second of all, if his opinion is sought about the security of the FRY, then Mr. Harmon needs to put that question correctly in terms of facts. If we are talking about a temporary transfer of 20- to 30.000 Muslims who were then taken to the territory of Tuzla and went further on to the FRY and if the murders took place in a period following the 13th of July, then he needs to tell the witness what information he has and whether the intelligence organ he is referring to had such information about the murders which took place in the area of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As suggested to me by Mr. Harmon [as interpreted], this is asking the same question, ask -- requiring of the witness to provide the same opinion about something that was put to him the first time around anyhow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, let me make a correction in the transcript at page 11, line 21: I did not make any suggestions to Mr. Lukic. I believe that was Mr. Guy-Smith who made a suggestion to Mr. Lukic. In respect of the objection, this witness is -- we've heard lots of testimony in this court about intelligence, intelligence reporting from the different armies within the armies. This witness has given evidence that, frankly, is quite surprising, that there was no -- that he would not expect this VJ intelligence officer to give information to the VJ Intelligence Administration about what were exceptionally dramatic and dangerous events for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And I am testing him with the question that I asked. And I put it in a hypothetical situation as to whether he, as a general officer of the Yugoslav Army in the same position, would have remained silent. And I think that's a perfectly proper question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question is: Where does it go, actually? What does the answer to that question -- where does it take you to?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It may take me, Your Honour, to his credibility, directly to his credibility, in answering the question in the way that he has answered the previous question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You're seeking opinion evidence from this witness. One, he's not an expert. I think for me I would expect you to confront him with evidence that shows that Jankovic did report, if indeed he did report, and say: Well, you're saying he was not -- he was resubordinated, but here it is, he sent reports to you guys. But a hypothetical question, I don't know what it does to the guilt or innocence of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: As I say, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It can only be his opinion. It's not fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm offering the question first of all on the issue of his credibility. Two -- one, he's an experienced officer of the highest rank in the Yugoslav Army. He has testified -- as I say, we have heard evidence that there was normal reporting. He's also told us that he isn't in the intelligence administration, which I can accept. He's told us a lot of things that he wasn't and that he wasn't aware of. But we can draw an inference, Your Honour, from the evidence that we've heard and the allegiance that one would have naturally as a general, as a high-ranking officer, to alert superiors about an imminent and potential -- potentially serious risk to his country. And so I am putting it -- I'm testing his answer that there was no need to do this with his duty as an officer to do precisely that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't -- well, I still don't see how you test a man's credibility on a hypothetical situation. The way you test a man's credibility is to confront him with facts that are contrary to what he says. But I don't know -- if he answers: Well, I would have reported or I would not have reported, how does that affect his credibility? If putting a hypothetical situation to him you ask his opinion, whether his opinion is different from what actually took place on the ground has nothing to do with the price of butter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not believe, under the circumstances, that silence and inaction was what was logical, what was required of the duty of an officer who had been temporarily sent. And this officer who has testified has told this Chamber that essentially he had no duty or responsibility. I don't know his exact words. But he had no obligation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He was resubordinated to another --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: He was resubordinated. I think that's an evasive answer, Your Honour. And I think that the duty of a Yugoslav Army officer, under those circumstances, is precisely the opposite. If there is an imminent danger to his country, he has to report it. And this officer is an experienced officer, and I'm saying: Okay, let me put you, General Borovic, in Colonel Jankovic's shoes and see what you would have done. And if he -- if he says: I would have done nothing because that's what -- when one is resubordinated there's an absolute cement wall of communication with my unit where I'm going to return, then that's his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And then I think his answer as to whether or not Colonel Jankovic was silent and had no commitment or obligation to inform his superiors is questionable, frankly, and it goes directly to his credibility. And I think I'm entitled to question -- examine his answers and test the strength of his answers and the credibility of his answers. And I think the hypothetical question that I posed to him is a perfectly proper question to ask him under the circumstances. I defer to the Court, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. The Trial Chamber is going to rule. By majority, Moloto dissenting, the question will be allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may re-call the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General Borovic, I will repeat my question to you. Let me put you in the shoes of Colonel Jankovic. Let's assume that you were in Srebrenica on the 12th and 13th of July, 1995, and you, sir, were aware that the Srebrenica enclave had been taken over. You were aware that 25- to 35.000 Muslim inhabitants from the enclave were forcibly displaced. You were aware that thousands of Muslim inhabitants from that enclave had been murdered. Would you -- and you were aware of those events -- that those events had security implications for your country. Would you have remained silent?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I will answer your question precisely the way you put it. First of all, I would have found a way not to participate in any activities that would be in contravention with my moral and ethic principles. That is why I was sent in early retirement at 2.00 a.m. as the youngest of the generals. That is why I resigned from my position of the executive director of the Ministry of Defence when this was to be violated. That is why I submitted my resignation to the position of the director general or general manager of the oil industry Nis. I went to join a university staff again because I never wanted to do anything that would go against my principles, and I would never have taken place in any way in an operation you describe, the way you describe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, you didn't answer my question. My question was: Would you have remained silent under the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in those circumstances, but I definitely would not have remained silent; however, I would not have been there in the first place taking any part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now if we could return to Prosecution Exhibit 2696, which is the personnel file of Colonel Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And could we return to, let me see, the page that we examined before. Could I have page 8 of the B/C/S and English document ID 0422-2995 ET, page 2. Okay. Can we scroll up on the English version. The B/C/S version -- the Serbian version was fine. Could we go up on the -- down then. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So you see that we've already discussed, General, the entry with the 30th Personnel Centre. Have you located that again on the personnel file of Colonel Jankovic? Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see where it says temporarily deployed to the 30th Personnel Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Fine. That was merely to locate you on this. Because I want you to -- we want to find out what happened to Colonel Jankovic after his temporary assignment to Srebrenica. Can you tell us by looking at the next entry where Colonel Jankovic went after his temporary assignment to the 30th Personnel Centre?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have had a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Can you -- well, let me -- can you tell us, then, after having looked at this, where he went? He returned to the VJ; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He returned to the 2nd Administration and its sector for OSP with the Belgrade Garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What does OSP stand for?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operational Staff Affairs. It's the sector for Operational Staff Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And in the far right box, there's a reference to 20-28 GS and there's a date. What does GS stand for in this context?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Intelligence Administration of the General Staff of the VJ. That's what it says. The Intelligence Administration of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So are they the body that issued order 20-28, or was it the General Staff? I'm referring to the box on the far right, General Borovic, that has reference to 20-28 GS. Is that a General Staff order that brought Colonel Jankovic back to the VJ?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that. What number you said? 28?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, if you take a look at the box -- you see the portion that says "30th Personnel Centre temporarily assigned"? And if you go to the far right-hand side --

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you go to the first box, below the reference to the 30th Personnel Centre, you will see the numbers 20-28 GS 07/02/96. So this is a reflection that an order was issued to bring Colonel Jankovic back to the 2nd Administration; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And letters GS, what does that stand for?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It stands for a General Staff order dated the 2nd of December -- February, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page in the English only.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And for your reference, I'm going to direct you to the entries that are in the penultimate box to see what happened with Colonel Jankovic's career. Okay? You see that box, sir, where it --

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. In fact, just confirm this, if you would: Colonel Jankovic became the chief of the 2nd Department of the 1st Sector of the Surveillance Administration of the General Staff of the VJ in Belgrade. And if we go to the far right-hand side of that box, this is pursuant to an order 4-148 of the Chief of the General Staff dated the 28th of August, 1998; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. The Chief of the General Staff or -- issued and signed documents for people to be promoted to the rank of colonel following proposals made by the personnel administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the final entry I'd like to direct your attention to is the last entry. If you would just affirm what I say, if it's -- if I say it accurately, Colonel Jankovic was then appointed as the military envoy of the Yugoslav Army to the Embassy of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in China; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that this is what the document states. I wasn't aware of this. This is what we can find in the document, and I take it as accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And on the far right-hand corner we can see that that was pursuant to an order of the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ, order number 5-208 of the 2nd of November, 1999 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last entry is one year after General Perisic was dismissed and I see no relation between these two things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm merely trying to complete the record on the career trajectory of this officer. He -- of course, I'm not asserting that this was General Perisic's order -- in fact, it could not have been General Perisic's order. So I accept Mr. Lukic's assertion. I'm merely pointing out to the Court what happened to Colonel Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Objection overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I've finished with this document, Your Honour. I'd like to look at another document if I could, it's P2518.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Take a moment, General, to read this document.

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. This is a document - for the record it's dated the 23rd of May, 1995 - and it is -- we can see at the bottom it is sent by Chief of Staff of the VRS, General Milovanovic. And this, as we can see from the first paragraph, is -- and I'll read the first paragraph: "Based on actual demonstrated need for engaging certain officers of the VJ" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, let me -- I'll slow down -- start again and I'll slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: "Based on actual demonstrated need for engaging certain officers of the VJ in the commands and units of the VRS, please send the following officers to assist, pursuant to Article 58 of the Law on the Yugoslav Army ..." Now, sir, I want to focus on the first entry, Svetozar Kosoric, who was a lieutenant-colonel. And we can see what his current duty is identified as in this document, which is the chief of intelligence affairs organ of the 1st Armoured Brigade of the VJ Special Units Corps. And the request is to have him assigned as the chief of intelligence affairs department in the command of the Drina Corps in the VRS. Now, the VJ Special Units Corps, those -- again, is this particular entity the special units corps in which Svetozar Kosoric was serving, was that under the command of -- was that under the command of the VJ General Staff, Special Units Corps?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The unit was under the command of the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ, but competent professional administrations have responsibility within their specific remits vis-à-vis that type of personnel. They were all inside the professional remit of the 2nd Administration, and their -- and the Special Units Corps was basically under the 2nd Personnel [as interpreted] Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the last paragraph in this document, it indicates that -- actually, before we -- let me go to the last paragraph. It says: "These officers were interviewed, and they have expressed their readiness to be temporarily engaged" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A correction for the transcript. Page 20, line 24, the witness said "the 2nd Intelligence Administration," whereas in the transcript we have "personnel administration."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Borovic? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. -- thank you, Mr. Lukic. You may proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me read, slowly, the last paragraph, sir. "These officers were interviewed, and they have expressed their readiness to be temporarily engaged and sent to the above VRS commands, as long as their status is properly regulated and their assignments in VJ units are frozen." Okay. Now, let me ask you, in respect of this document -- I'd like you to identify, first of all, the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could scroll to see the top of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If you could identify the handwriting and the initials in the upper right-hand corner of this document, what does it say, sir? Whose initials are they?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, both the note and the initials were made by General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what does the note say? Can you read it?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "Summon and dispatch if they want to go; if they don't, a proposal."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we go to the bottom of the document in the -- yes. Up -- sorry, if we could move over. There's some handwriting. I'd like to capture the handwriting to the left of the stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know whose handwriting that is?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I can make it out. It says: "Submitted to Colonel-General Matovic on the 24th of May, awaiting an answer." Okay. Okay. Thank you. We're going to look at a film, General Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could have P438 on the monitor. We're going to start the film at 1:42:52, and we're going to end the film at 1:45:15. And it -- for the record, Your Honour, Colonel Kosoric has been identified in P438. The transcript citation is at 6569, starting at line 21. So if we could play this portion of the film.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The individual who Mr. Butler identified, just so Your Honours are clear, is the second person from the left, the man with the bald head and the moustache. That is Colonel Kosoric. So if we can continue playing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, Colonel Kosoric is the individual at the far right in this image. He's the bald man, again, with the moustache. I've stopped the film at 1:45:11.8. That's what I need to play.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, sir, following the completion of --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me just make one other reference to the record. There is testimony in the record that -- from Mr. Butler, found at page 6.570 at lines 6 and 7, that Colonel Kosoric served as the chief of the intelligence department of the Drina Corps command, so the -- just connecting what the request was and what the facts before this Trial Chamber are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you recall that following the completion of Colonel Kosoric's assignment to the VRS that he left his post in the VRS and he went to the VMA, the medical centre, and he did not report to his duty in the new assigned post in the VRS and that General Milovanovic sent General Perisic personally a letter, requesting that Kosoric be returned to the VRS and that that request of General Milovanovic was forwarded by the General Staff -- was received by the General Staff and was forwarded to the office of General Matovic. Do you remember your office receiving such a letter about Colonel Kosoric?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prosecutor, sir, I don't remember, but it probably happened that way. We should look into where this request came from, who sent it to General Matovic. I don't know Colonel Kosoric, and I don't remember anything related to him. We can look at a document from the cabinet and who signed it, but I can't recall that now because I don't even know that colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can I have XN 431 on the monitor, please. What I'm interested on this document is English e-court 0677-9830 page 1 and B/C/S page 74.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's the purpose?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I can have just a minute, Your Honour. I just need to check one thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At this point, Your Honour, what I'd like to do is just show the document to the witness. He may recall, after seeing the document. This may refresh his recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That was just to jog his memory?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Can I assume, Mr. Lukic, that your nodding of the head is an indication of agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is not the document that I asked -- that I want on the screen. Let me repeat: It's 06 - this might be the numbers - but it's 0677-9830, page 1 of the English e-court version -- Let me just get some correction on this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is the correct version on the document -- of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I want you to take a look at this, if you would, sir. Would you just take a look at the letter in your language, and if the Court -- once the Court has an opportunity --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is a two-page or a three-page document in English. If we can turn to the next page in English so that the Trial Chamber can see the English text. And if this English version can also be scrolled up so the stamp and the text at the bottom can be seen. And then if we can go to the third page of the English version, we can see a name there. So if we can go back to the first page of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document -- you can see from this document that it is dated the 19th of May, 1996, from the Main Staff of the VRS, and it -- you have seen earlier it is from General Milovanovic. You can see that on your text. And you can see some --

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you can see from the text of the document - if we can go to the second page in the English - we can see from this -- and we need to see --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We can see from the text of this document that Mr. Svetozar Kosoric was seconded from the VRS and he held the post of chief of the intelligence department in the Drina Corps command. And when that corps, the Drina Corps, was disbanded, he was given a new post but he went to the medical centre and he hasn't reported to his newly assigned post. Now, let me, first of all, confirm some things with you, sir. This document was received by the Yugoslav Army General Staff, office of the Chief of the General Staff, as reflected in the stamp in the lower left-hand corner of the document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And could we scroll to see the bottom of the B/C/S version or the Serbian version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We can see, at the bottom, sir, some text with a stamp and a name and a signature. Can you, first of all, read the text to us.

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The text says: "To the commander of the special unit corps of the Army of Yugoslavia, we request an urgent proposal to the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, and this Officer IJ," which stands for Ivan Jevtovic, signed for the chief. He was my assistant for planning and operations. When he received it in the cabinet, he didn't do anything about it. He didn't take any action. We can scroll back up to see what other suggestions were made --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- this assistant of mine sent it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm going to go there in just a minute, but I want to just develop one other element of the stamp at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can we go down to the bottom of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And we see -- does your name appear on -- as the person whose name appears at the bottom, even though this may have been signed by some -- your assistant? Is your name on this?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name of the superior officer is always typed, but the person who stands in for him can sign if the superior officer is absent. I was very much involved in everything that was -- that concerned the reorganisation, and I was often away from the office. I'm not evading my responsibility, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... my question -- could you just -- if you just listen to my question. Does your name appear on this document at that location?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in the typed version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And I accept that your assistant signed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could go up to the upper right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You and I wanted to go to the same notation of this document. And can you identify in this document -- first of all, in the top handwriting that's at a diagonal, whose handwriting is that and what does it say?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The handwriting that goes diagonally is that of General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what does it say?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This first word is difficult to make out. The second word, however, is "proposal," so it must be "prepare a proposal," but it's not very legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Then we see some other handwriting at the -- below General Perisic's handwriting. Can you read what that says?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, let me stop you there because I'm not getting any interpretation. I could hear it in Serbian, but I couldn't hear it in English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's mistake. Microphone was off.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So let me ask you, General Borovic, to repeat. Could you start reading the language that's handwritten and with -- there's a signature underneath it. What does it say?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, at the top in the right-hand corner, it says Colonel Mijic slash something. And then below it says: "At the collegium of the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia on the 10th of June, 1996, it was decided that he return to the 30th Personnel Centre," signed J. Mijic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time and this would be -- I can continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take the break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have on the -- this is a document, Your Honour, that is related to the document we just examined, XN 431. It's part of XN 431. So if I could have e-court English 0677-9829 ET, and the Serbian language version at page 73, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we still in the mode of a memory refreshment?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right, General Borovic, you can see the Serbian-language version in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could have the English-language version centred and scrolled down a little bit. And if we could have it centred, that would be helpful. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document that relates to the request of General Milovanovic. And we can see from this document, can we not, that this is a communication that is directed to the sector for recruitment, mobilisation, and systems issues, specifically to Lieutenant-General Matovic in respect of the VRS proposal. And it is a request that the sector for recruitment, mobilisation, and systems issue prepare a proposal that relates to General Milovanovic's request. Do you confirm that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And we can see a time-stamp at the bottom. This is the 27th of May, 1996, and then there is a stamp and a signature line. Does your name at least appear on the signature line?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My name is typed there, and the actual signature is by my deputy, Colonel Vlajkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, let me ask you, then, in respect of the two documents I have shown you, we have first of all the document from General Milovanovic that was received by the cabinet on the 21st of May, 1996, and it was forwarded by your assistant to the commander of the special units corps. And then we can see that a second communication in respect of the VRS request was forwarded to Lieutenant-General Matovic. And we can see that there was -- a proposal was drafted, and, in fact, this matter was decided at a collegium. Now, deciding a matter like this at a collegium, whether to transfer somebody back to the VRS, would be unusual, would it not? In other words, those matters were usually decided in the absence of a decision of the highest-ranking generals of the General Staff to make a decision?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, if General Risto Matovic, the assistant, believes that the proposal should be submitted to the collegium, then he drafts that proposal; if not, then he would decide it within his competences because he is the chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: But my question is this: Deciding a matter like this, in other words, to return Colonel Kosoric to the VRS, that was a matter that was decided at the collegium, the highest body of officers of the General Staff. Was that the usual procedure, or was that something that was quite unusual?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that was decided at the collegium, it would be an unusual procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, having seen all of these documents and having seen, sir, that this decision, there was a decision taken at the collegium, having seen that these documents passed through your office, do these documents that I'm showing you refresh your recollection as to the circumstances regarding the request relating to General -- to Colonel Kosoric?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I did not see, among the documents, the decision of the collegium, but none of this refreshes my memory regarding Colonel Kosoric.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In that case, Your Honour, I will not seek the admission of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You do not seek?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I asked that these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- be used for purposes of trying to refresh the witness's recollection. He's seen these, he's examined these, it doesn't refresh his recollection. I'm not seeking their admission, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have concluded my examination of General Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General Borovic, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I would like to, before I sit down, regulate Exhibit XN 446, which was deferred. I will not seek the admission of XN 446.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. XN 446, okay. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the Court's indulgence, Your Honours, to organise my papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have the indulgence, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you on the subjects covered by Mr. Harmon yesterday and earlier today. The first area is, in fact, the first thing Mr. Harmon asked you, about the time when you were appointed chef de cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To make this completely clear, I would like one document to be placed on the ELMO just to refresh the witness's memory. I will not tender it. We did not use the personnel file of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you show it to Mr. Harmon first. Ma'am, could you please show it to Mr. Harmon before you put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is only in Serbian, an excerpt from the personnel file of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There was some confusion about the time when you were appointed, and that confusion arose probably from my questions, the time when you were appointed chef de cabinet of the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. This document is only in Serbian, General, so the other participants in the courtroom cannot follow. But just tell us, do you see from this document when -- first of all, what are we looking at, and when were you appointed chef de cabinet of the Chief of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: SINISA BOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, when I answered this question I said I thought it was in November and counsel said it was in December. This says that by virtue of order 3-326 of 24th of November, 1994, I was appointed - this is the peacetime phrasing - I was appointed chef de cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I was a bit confusing about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not seeking admission, Your Honours. I just wanted the witness to be clear about the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The second area Mr. Harmon questioned you about is the visit of the military delegation to Russia, the delegation which included the Defence Minister Mr. Bulatovic, and General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have Prosecution Exhibit P761 [In English] P6 -- 761 -- [Interpretation] Now I see that this document is under seal, so we need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P719, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before us are the minutes of the 34th Session of the Supreme Defence Council held on 2 March 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next page, please, in both versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I raise the same objection I raised previously. This witness, I understood his evidence to be, he was not present at the SDC meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This question is in the same vein, refreshing his recollection, which I did with the previous document as well. But that document happened before the visit.
